In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effective temperature scale for B-type stars has not yet been established and that the situation is further complicated by a metallicity dependence.

the LMC and SMC stars have higher surface nitrogen abundances than their Galactic counterparts, that the LMC stars have higher nitrogen abundances than the SMC, and that there is an increase in the nitrogen abundances with increasing effective temperature in all three galaxies.

the temperature scales of B-type dwarfs and supergiants are not well understood and that further theoretical and observational work is needed in order to fully understand the effects of stellar rotation, binarity and metallicity on the evolution of B-type stars.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the LMC is the most similar to the Galaxy with a similar effective temperature scale and a similar nitrogen enhancement in the most massive stars.
the Galactic B-type dwarf stars have effective temperatures 300-500K higher than their LMC and SMC counterp arts.
the stars in the Magellanic Cloud clusters have similar atmospheric parameters to their Galactic counterparts but with slightly lower effective temperatures and higher gravities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
rotation plays an important role in the evolution of massive stars.
the nitrogen abundances in the B-type stars in all 4 fields show a clear trend with rotational velocity.

the nitrogen abundances of B-type stars show a clear correlation with their rotational velocities, with slow rotators having a wide range of N abundances and fast rotators having a much more restricted distribution.
